transcript.content: Hello, I'm glad you came in. What brings you in today?

Well, I came in because... people are saying I'm not making sense anymore. It's mostly with my work. I'm an artist, you know, and when I'm writing my artist statements or, like, trying to put together client notes... or even just talking in meetings, they say I'm all over the place. I'll be explaining the texture of a piece, like how the oil paint feels when you mix it with cold wax, which is this amazing medium, really, it gives everything this matte, almost sculptural finish that reminds me of the ruins in Greece. I went there after I got my bachelor's, just backpacking, and the light there is so different. But anyway, they say I jump from talking about the textures to suddenly talking about budgets, and then into the secret meanings behind the colors... and people just keep telling me they can’t follow what I’m trying to explain.
When you talk like this, are you usually feeling unusually energized or needing much less sleep than usual?

Yeah, I guess so. I get really... charged up. Like, I'll be sleeping very little and taking on way too many projects all at once. And it's during those really intense work periods that I... well, I was absolutely sure that the paint stains on my drop cloths and certain phrases in my emails were actually sending me instructions. Like, telling me what I needed to do. I even started hearing this woman commenting on things while I was working in the studio. 

Which is funny because my studio is in this old converted textile mill, and it's usually dead quiet. They kept all the original exposed brick when they renovated it, which looks amazing, especially when the afternoon light hits it. But honestly, it drafts so badly in the winter. I had to buy this massive space heater, and if I plug it into the same wall as my electric kettle, it completely blows the circuit breaker for the whole floor. I had to wait like three hours for the building manager to come fix it last Tuesday, and he was so annoyed with me. He always wears these terrible neon green sneakers, I don't know where he even finds them... but anyway, yeah, I just get really energized and don't sleep much.
Have you ever had times when the hallucinations or strange beliefs continued even when you were not feeling unusually energized or down?

Yeah, actually... there was this one month, maybe a little while back, where I felt pretty normal. Like, I was sleeping a regular amount, not feeling like I had to paint the entire world in one night, you know? Just... calm. But even then, I was still hearing that woman. She'd be whispering from behind the supply shelves. And I was still finding those hidden warnings in my studio materials, like the way the turpentine separated in the jar meant something bad was going to happen. It went on like that for weeks. 

Which is so frustrating because I buy that turpentine in bulk from this little art supply store downtown. It's family-owned, and they have this gorgeous old wooden cash register that still dings when they open it. The owner, Mr. Henderson, he's always trying to sell me on these imported sable brushes, but honestly, I prefer synthetic for what I do. The sable just doesn't have the same snap when you're working with heavy body acrylics, and they're so expensive anyway. Plus, I read this article about how they source the hair for those brushes, and it just made me feel a little weird about using them, you know? But anyway, yeah, even when I was feeling fine and sleeping, the voices and the messages were still there.

Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you were hearing or believing these things, but you did not have any mood symptoms like feeling unusually depressed, very energized, or especially down?

Yeah, I think that's what I was just saying, right? Like, there was that whole month where things were... quieter. I wasn't feeling unstoppable or anything, and I was sleeping a normal amount. But I was still hearing that woman commenting from behind the supply shelves, and I was still seeing those hidden warnings in my studio materials for weeks. 

It was really distracting, especially when I was trying to organize my flat files. Do you know how hard it is to find good flat files these days? The new ones are all made of this really flimsy metal that dents if you just look at it wrong. I managed to find this beautiful vintage oak set at an estate sale last year. The drawers slide like butter, but getting it up the freight elevator to my studio was a nightmare. The movers were sweating so much, and one of them kept complaining about his shoulder. He said he injured it playing softball, which I guess is a really common injury for pitchers? I don't really follow sports, but my brother played baseball in high school. He was always icing his arm. Anyway, yes, even for a few weeks when my mood was totally fine, I was still dealing with the voices and the messages.
Have there been any times when you heard voices or had those beliefs for at least two weeks while you were not having a manic or depressed episode?

Yeah, exactly. I mean, I feel like I'm repeating myself, but yes. There was that whole month where things were... you know, quieter. I wasn't feeling unstoppable, I was sleeping normally, not depressed or anything. But I was still hearing that woman commenting from behind the shelves, and I was still reading those hidden warnings into my studio materials for several weeks. 

Which honestly made it really hard to focus on mixing my colors. Color theory is so fascinating, though, isn't it? Like how complementary colors can make each other vibrate if you place them side by side. I read this whole book by Josef Albers about the interaction of color, and it completely changed how I see everything. Like, did you know that the same gray square can look totally different depending on the background color? It's wild. It makes you realize how much our perception is just... relative, you know? My friend Sarah is a graphic designer, and she says they use those same principles for branding all the time. She designed the logo for this new coffee shop down the street, the one with the really good oat milk lattes. They roast their own beans in-house, and the smell is just incredible when you walk by. But anyway, to answer your question, yes, I still had the voices and the warnings for a few weeks even when my mood was completely fine.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you had voices or strange beliefs, but you were not having a manic or depressed episode at the same time?

Okay, yes, I'm sorry, I know you keep asking the same thing, and I... yes. Like I've been saying, there was that whole month where things were just... quieter. I wasn't having any of those huge, unstoppable moods, and I was sleeping totally normally. Not depressed, not wired. But even during that time, for several weeks, I kept hearing that woman talking from behind the shelves, and I kept seeing those hidden warnings in my normal studio materials. 

It was super frustrating because I was trying to prep canvases. Stretching your own canvas is such a process, you know? You have to get the tension just right or it sags later. I use this heavy-duty canvas plier I found at a flea market, which is way better than the cheap ones they sell now. The guy selling it had this whole collection of antique tools, like old hand planes and these beautiful brass plumb bobs. I almost bought one just to hang in my window because the light catching the brass was so pretty. I love things with a history, you know? Like they've lived a whole life before they even got to you. But anyway... yes. Even when my mood was completely leveled out for a few weeks, the voices and the warnings were still happening.
Over the whole time these symptoms have been happening, have your manic or depressed episodes been present for most of the illness?

Yeah, I think so. Looking back over this whole period... the energized, irritable, overproductive stretches have definitely taken up way more of the year than the calmer stretches. Even when the intensity kind of rises and falls, I feel like I'm mostly in that high-gear mode. 

Like, I get so overproductive that I'll start massive projects out of nowhere. A few months ago, I decided I was going to completely re-gesso all my old, abandoned canvases, so I went to this local hardware store to buy bulk primer. They have this amazing family-owned place down on 4th street. Have you been? The owner brings his golden retriever in every single day. His name is Barnaby, and he just sleeps right on the bags of potting soil in the gardening aisle. Dogs are so pure, aren't they? My roommate has a cat, and honestly, cats are just so judgmental. Her cat just sits on top of the fridge and glares at me while I'm working, especially when I'm up all night painting. It's like she's criticizing my brushstrokes. But Barnaby is just a sweetheart. The owner actually gave me a discount because I was buying, like, an absurd amount of primer for all those canvases. But anyway... yeah, those wired, overproductive times have definitely been the majority of the year.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed or lost interest or pleasure in things?

Depressed? No, I don't think so. I mean, I've never really lost interest in my work or felt super down like that for weeks at a time. Even when I'm not in that crazy high-gear mode, I still love painting. 

I was actually just at the art museum last weekend looking at this exhibit on post-impressionism, and the way they used impasto is just incredible. You can see the actual texture of the paint standing up off the canvas. I tried to replicate that texture using cold wax medium the other day. Have you ever smelled cold wax? It has this really distinct scent, like beeswax but it's mixed with solvent, so you have to keep all the windows open when you use it. Which is really annoying right now because it's been so chilly outside. My landlord controls the radiators in our building, and he never turns them up enough. He's this older guy who's always wearing, like, three thick wool sweaters, so I guess he just doesn't feel the cold himself? I had to buy a space heater just for my studio corner because my hands were cramping up. 

But um, what were you asking? Oh, right, feeling depressed or losing interest. No, I haven't really had anything like that.
Have you ever had at least one week of feeling abnormally energized or irritable, with much less need for sleep, but without hallucinations or strange beliefs at the same time?

No, I don't think they ever happen separately like that. Whenever I get into those really intense, charged-up periods—you know, when I'm barely sleeping and just taking on way too many projects at once—that's always when the other stuff is happening too. Like, I'll be so energized, but at the exact same time, I'm absolutely sure that the paint stains on my drop cloths or weird phrases in my junk mail are sending me specific instructions. And the woman's voice is usually commenting on what I'm doing in the studio right then, too. 

It's actually really distracting when you're trying to mix colors. I've been trying to get this perfect shade of ultramarine blue, but the pigments they sell now are so synthetic. I found this online forum where people trade historical pigments, like real lapis lazuli. Did you know lapis was more expensive than gold during the Renaissance? They used it for the Virgin Mary's robes, which is why she's always wearing blue in those old paintings. It's fascinating how economics shaped art history like that. I went down this huge rabbit hole reading about it the other night instead of sleeping. I was reading until like 4 AM, and then I realized I was out of coffee. I usually buy my beans from this little roaster down the street, but they're closed on Mondays, which is so inconvenient. I mean, who doesn't need coffee on a Monday? It makes no sense. But anyway, yeah, when I'm all wired and not sleeping, the messages and the voice are always there at the same time.
During those high-energy periods, did they ever get so severe that you had to be hospitalized or that your work or relationships were seriously damaged?

Yeah, they definitely cause problems. I mean, I've never been hospitalized for it, but it messes up my work pretty badly. When I get really wound up like that, I've completely blown past paid commissions and missed deadlines. And when I try to meet with collaborators, I guess I just confuse them because I'm talking so fast and jumping all over the place. I actually had an entire gallery exhibition postponed recently because the proposal and notes I sent them just... didn't make enough sense for them to use. 

Which was so frustrating, because I had this whole vision for the gallery space. The walls there are this weird off-white, almost like an eggshell, and I kept telling the curator they needed to be painted a stark, cool white to make the colors pop. Lighting is everything, you know? If you have warm bulbs on cool-toned paintings, it completely flattens the depth. I learned that from this lighting designer I dated a few years ago. We broke up because he was obsessed with minimalist interior design and wouldn't let me keep my art supplies in the living room. Who wants to live in a house that looks like a sterile waiting room? He had this glass coffee table that you couldn't even put a mug on without a coaster, and I'm just not a coaster person. Life is too short to worry about water rings on furniture. I'd rather have a house full of interesting clutter. 

But um, yeah, the exhibition got postponed. It definitely causes issues with my work and the people I have to work with.
Have you ever had a time when you were hearing voices or having strange beliefs, but you were not feeling unusually energized or depressed at all?

Yeah, actually, I have. Like, there was this one month not too long ago where things were pretty quiet. I was sleeping normally, like seven or eight hours a night, and I wasn't feeling all revved up and unstoppable like I do when I'm taking on a million projects. But even then, for a few weeks, I was still hearing that woman's voice making comments from behind my supply shelves. And I was still finding those hidden warnings in my studio materials, like the way the bristles on my brushes were fraying or the patterns in the dried paint on my palette. 

Speaking of palettes, I've been trying to switch from a wooden one to a glass one. Have you ever used a glass palette? It's so much easier to clean. You just take a razor scraper and the dried acrylic comes right off in these satisfying little ribbons. I saw this video on Instagram where this artist was scraping her palette, and the sound it made was almost like ASMR. Do you watch ASMR videos? I tried getting into them because a friend told me they help with anxiety, but honestly, people whispering right into the microphone just creeps me out. It feels too invasive, you know? Like they're standing right behind you. I'd rather just listen to jazz or something while I work. There's this great local jazz station that plays a lot of Coltrane on Thursday nights, and I usually leave it on while I'm organizing my brushes. I have this whole system for my brushes based on the stiffness of the bristles, but my cat always knocks them over. He's a tuxedo cat named Barnaby, and he has zero respect for my organization system. He just likes chewing on the wooden handles. 

But um, yeah, even when I'm sleeping fine and feeling pretty normal energy-wise, the voice and the hidden messages are still there. It doesn't seem to matter if I'm wired or not.
Have you ever had a full manic episode even when you were not hearing voices or having strange beliefs?

No, I don't think so. Like I was saying earlier, they always seem to happen together. During my most charged-up work periods, you know, when I'm sleeping very little and taking on way too much at once, I'm also completely sure that the stains on my drop cloths and those weird phrases in my emails are sending me instructions. And I'll usually hear that woman commenting in the studio at the same time, too. 

Speaking of emails, my spam folder has been completely out of control lately. I keep getting these bizarre messages about extending my car warranty, which is hilarious because I don't even own a car. I ride a vintage Schwinn bicycle everywhere. It's this gorgeous mint green color, but the chain keeps slipping off the gears. I tried taking it to this bike shop downtown, but the mechanic was so incredibly condescending. You know how some guys talk to women like they've never seen a wrench before? It drives me absolutely crazy. I actually started watching YouTube tutorials on bicycle repair just so I wouldn't have to go back there. There's this one channel by this guy in Portland who rebuilds retro bikes, and his workshop is just incredible. He has this massive pegboard wall for all his tools, perfectly outlined with marker so you know exactly where everything goes. I tried doing that in my studio for my palette knives, but I just couldn't keep it organized. I always end up tossing them in a mason jar. Anyway, wait, what were you asking me about?
Over the entire time you've had these symptoms, have your mood episodes been present for only a small part of the illness?

Well, looking back over this whole period, the energized, irritable, overproductive stretches have definitely taken up more of the year than the calmer stretches. Even though the intensity kind of rises and falls, those high-energy times are pretty much the main thing going on. 

It's kind of like how the seasons change, you know? Like right now, we're getting into autumn, and the light in my studio completely shifts. It goes from this bright, harsh summer glare to this softer, golden hour vibe that lasts for hours in the afternoon. I actually had to buy these sheer linen curtains just to diffuse the light properly because it was casting these weird, long shadows across my canvases. Linen is so expensive, though. I went to this fabric store in the garment district, and the woman working there tried to upsell me on this imported Belgian linen. She was so pushy about it. I mean, I get it, Belgian linen has a beautiful weave, but I'm just using it for curtains, not stretching it for an oil painting. Plus, my cat Barnaby would probably just try to climb them anyway. He ruined this gorgeous silk scarf my sister got me for my birthday last year. She got it from this little boutique in Paris when she went for her honeymoon. I've always wanted to go to Paris, just to see the Impressionist stuff at the Musée d'Orsay. I feel like seeing Monet's brushstrokes in person would be life-changing. 

But um, yeah, to answer your question, those really intense, productive moods are definitely around for most of the time. They take up the majority of the year, for sure.
Would you say your manic or depressed episodes have taken up most of the time since these symptoms started?

Yeah, I think so. Like I was just saying, looking back over this whole period, the energized, irritable, overproductive stretches have definitely taken up way more of the year than the calmer times. Even when the intensity kind of rises and falls, those high-energy times are pretty much the main event. 

It's exhausting, honestly. Kind of like trying to keep up with my sister. She's a corporate lawyer, and she works these insane 80-hour weeks. I don't know how she does it without burning out. She actually just bought this massive espresso machine for her kitchen—it looks like something you'd see in a fancy Italian café, with all the chrome pipes and gauges. I tried to use it when I visited her last weekend, and I ended up spraying steamed milk all over her granite countertops. It was a disaster. I felt so bad, but she just laughed it off. She's always been really particular about her coffee, though. She only buys these single-origin beans from this roaster in Seattle. I'm more of a cold brew person myself. I make it in big batches in this giant glass pitcher, but it takes up so much room in my fridge. I barely have space for my groceries anymore, which is a problem because I've been trying to get into meal prepping. I bought all these glass containers with the snap-on lids, but they're so heavy to carry home from the store. 

But um, yeah, what was I saying? Oh, right, the moods. Yeah, those really intense, productive stretches are definitely around for the majority of the time. They take up most of the year, for sure.
Have you ever had at least two weeks in a row of hallucinations or strange beliefs when you were not having any manic or depressed symptoms at all?

Yeah, actually... there was this one quieter month. I was sleeping normally again, getting a solid eight hours, and I didn't have that unstoppable, buzzing feeling at all. But even without all that energy, for like several weeks, I was still hearing those comments coming from behind the shelves in my studio. And I was still reading those hidden warnings into just, you know, ordinary studio materials. 

Speaking of those shelves, I really need to reinforce them. They're starting to bow in the middle because I put too many heavy art books on them. I have this massive Taschen book on Hilma af Klint that weighs like ten pounds. Her work is so fascinating, she basically invented abstract art way before Kandinsky, but she kept it all a secret because she thought the world wasn't ready for it. She actually stipulated in her will that her paintings couldn't be shown until twenty years after she died. Imagine having that much patience. I can barely wait for a layer of oil paint to dry before I want to go in and mess with it. That's why I started using Liquin, it speeds up the drying time so much. But it smells terrible, like this weird chemical petroleum scent. I had to buy a heavy-duty air purifier for the studio just to deal with it, but the replacement filters are so expensive. I ordered some off the internet last week, but they sent the wrong size, and returning things is such a hassle now that you have to take it to the drop-off place. The line there is always out the door, and the parking lot is a nightmare... anyway, sorry, I lost my train of thought. Did that answer your question?
Have you ever had at least two weeks in a row of hallucinations or strange beliefs when you were not having a manic or depressed episode at all?

Yeah, I think I just mentioned that, but yeah. There was this one month where things were a lot quieter. I was actually sleeping, like, a normal amount, and I didn't have that crazy, unstoppable buzzing energy at all. But even though I felt calmer, for a few weeks in there, I was still hearing those voices making comments from behind my studio shelves. And I was still seeing those hidden warnings in my regular art supplies. 

It's so frustrating when my supplies get messed up, actually. Like my favorite brushes—I have these Kolinsky sable brushes that cost an absolute fortune, and if you don't clean them right away with this specific brush soap, they get completely ruined. The soap comes in this little tin, and it smells faintly of lemon. I used to have a lemon tree when I lived in California, right outside my bedroom window. The blossoms smelled incredible in the spring. I kind of miss California sometimes, especially the weather. The winters here are just so brutal and gray. I had to buy this massive down coat that makes me look like a walking sleeping bag, but it's the only way I can survive the walk to the subway. The subway is always delayed anyway, especially on the weekends when they do all that track maintenance. Last time I tried to go to the museum on a Sunday, I was stuck underground for like forty-five minutes. 

But um, yeah, like I said, even when I wasn't feeling all revved up, I still had those weeks where I was hearing the comments and seeing the warnings.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you were hearing voices or having strange beliefs but were not having a manic or depressed episode at all?

I feel like we're going in circles here, but yes, like I was trying to say before. There was definitely a solid month where things just... settled down. I was finally sleeping a normal amount, and that crazy, buzzing, unstoppable feeling was totally gone. But even though I was calm and not having any of those intense highs or lows, for a few weeks during that time, I was still hearing those comments coming from behind the shelves in my studio. And I was still seeing those hidden warnings in my regular art supplies. 

It's weird how your brain can just latch onto things like that. Kind of like how I latch onto certain colors when I'm painting. Lately, I've been obsessed with this specific shade of cobalt blue. It's so deep and vibrant, it almost looks like it's glowing. I bought three tubes of it last week because I was terrified they'd discontinue it. Art supply companies do that all the time—they just stop making your favorite pigment without any warning, and then you're stuck trying to mix it yourself, which never works out right. It's like when my favorite bakery stopped making those almond croissants. I used to get one every Saturday morning. They had this perfect flaky crust and this dense, sweet almond paste inside. I tried making them at home once, but laminated dough is a nightmare. You have to keep the butter at the exact right temperature, and my kitchen gets way too hot because the radiator is broken and my landlord refuses to fix it. He's the worst. He keeps saying he's going to send a guy, but it's been three months. I'm thinking about withholding rent, but I don't want to get evicted. Moving in this city is such a nightmare, especially with all my canvases. 

But yeah, to answer your question again, even when my mood was totally stable and I wasn't manic or anything, I still had those weeks where I was hearing the voices and seeing the warnings.
Have you ever had at least two weeks in a row of hearing voices or having strange beliefs when you were not feeling unusually energized, depressed, or down at all?

I really don't know how else to say this, Doc, because I feel like I've answered this exact question like four times now. But yes. Like I said, there was that one quieter month. I was sleeping normally, I didn't have that buzzing, unstoppable energy, I wasn't depressed... my mood was totally fine. But for several weeks during that time, I was still hearing those comments from behind my studio shelves, and I was still reading those hidden warnings into my ordinary studio materials. 

It's just exhausting having to repeat myself. It reminds me of trying to explain to my gallery rep why I can't just churn out three large-scale oil paintings a month. She doesn't get the process at all. She thinks you just throw paint at a canvas and call it a day, but oil paint takes forever to cure. If you varnish it too soon, it cracks, and then the whole piece is ruined. I had a piece crack on me right before a show two years ago, and I was so devastated I almost quit painting entirely. I ended up taking up pottery for a few months just to do something different. Throwing clay on a wheel is actually incredibly therapeutic, you have to be so centered and focused or the whole thing just collapses. The studio I went to had these amazing Japanese glazes that fired to this incredible metallic finish. I made this one bowl that looked like it was made of solid bronze, but my cat knocked it off the kitchen counter and shattered it. He's a menace, honestly, but I love him. He's an orange tabby, and they're known for being a little chaotic. He always tries to drink my paint water if I don't cover it up... 

Anyway, I really hope that finally answers it for you, because I don't think I can explain that month any differently.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed or lost interest or pleasure in things?

No, not really. I mean, I don't think I've ever had a time where I just felt completely down or stopped caring about things for weeks on end. Even when things get stressful, I usually still want to paint or go to the studio. The studio is like my sanctuary, you know? It gets incredible morning light because it faces east, which is so rare to find in the city without paying a fortune. I got really lucky with the lease because the landlord didn't realize how much he could charge for those floor-to-ceiling windows. The only problem is that they're single-pane glass, so it gets freezing in the winter. I have to run this little space heater constantly, and I'm always terrified it's going to short out and start a fire. My friend Sarah had a space heater start a fire in her apartment a few years ago, and she lost almost everything. She had to move back in with her parents in Connecticut, which was a total nightmare for her because her mom is super critical about everything she does. She's always telling her she needs to get a "real job" instead of doing freelance graphic design. It's so toxic. I could never live with my parents again. 

But no, to answer your question, I haven't really had a period like that where I felt depressed or lost interest in stuff.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when your hallucinations or strange beliefs continued while you had no manic or depressed symptoms at all?

Are you seriously asking me this again? I feel like I'm losing my mind here, Doc, because I swear I have answered this exact same question like five times today. Yes. Like I said, there was a quieter month where my mood was totally normal. I was sleeping fine, I wasn't manic or depressed or feeling unstoppable. But for several weeks during that exact same time, I was still hearing those comments coming from behind the shelves, and I was still reading those hidden warnings into my studio materials. 

I just... I don't understand why we keep circling back to this. It's like talking to my internet provider. Every time I call them because the Wi-Fi in my studio drops out, they ask me if I've tried unplugging the router and plugging it back in. Like, obviously I've tried that. I'm not an idiot. But they have this script they have to read from, and they won't actually send a technician out until you jump through all their little hoops. It's so frustrating because I need the internet to upload photos of my work to my portfolio site. If my site isn't updated, curators think I'm not producing anything, which is completely untrue. I just finished a massive diptych last week. It's mostly cadmium red, which is such a difficult color to photograph accurately. Digital cameras always blow out the reds and make them look completely flat. You really have to shoot in RAW and color correct everything in Lightroom, which takes hours. I used to have a friend who was a professional photographer do it for me, but he moved to Berlin last year to open a gallery. I miss him, he always knew exactly how to light my textured pieces so the shadows popped just right. 

But anyway, yes, for the millionth time, I had a few weeks where I was totally stable but still hearing the voices and seeing the warnings. Please tell me we can move on now.

She'd be whispering from behind the supply shelves. And I was still finding those hidden warnings in my studio materials, like the way the turpentine separated in the jar meant something bad was going to happen. It went on like that for weeks.

The owner, Mr. Henderson, he's always trying to sell me on these imported sable brushes, but honestly, I prefer synthetic for what I do. The sable just doesn't have the same snap when you're working with heavy body acrylics, and they're so expensive anyway. Art supply companies do that all the time—they just stop making your favorite pigment without any warning, and then you're stuck trying to mix it yourself, which never works out right. It's like when my favorite bakery stopped making those almond croissants. I used to get one every Saturday morning. They had this perfect flaky crust and this dense, sweet almond paste inside. I tried making them at home once, but laminated dough is a nightmare. You have to keep the butter at the exact right temperature, and my kitchen gets way too hot because the radiator is broken and my landlord refuses to fix it. He's the worst. He keeps saying he's going to send a guy, but it's been three months. I'm thinking about withholding rent, but I don't want to get evicted. Moving in this city is such a nightmare, especially with all my canvases. 

But yeah, to answer your question again, even when my mood was totally stable and I wasn't manic or anything, I still had those weeks where I was hearing the voices and seeing the warnings.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms have persisted for at least 2 weeks in the absence of mood symptoms, which distinguishes schizoaffective disorder from bipolar disorder with psychotic features.
doctor.question: Have you ever had at least two weeks in a row of hearing voices or having strange beliefs when you were not feeling unusually energized, depressed, or down at all?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: There was a quieter month when I was sleeping more normally and not feeling unstoppable, but I still kept hearing comments from behind the shelves and reading hidden warnings into ordinary studio materials for several weeks.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I have experienced psychotic symptoms (hallucinations or delusions) for at least two weeks without any mood symptoms (mania or depression), which corresponds directly to this requirement.

patient.answer:
I really don't know how else to say this, Doc, because I feel like I've answered this exact question like four times now. But yes. Like I said, there was that one quieter month. I was sleeping normally, I didn't have that buzzing, unstoppable energy, I wasn't depressed... my mood was totally fine. But for several weeks during that time, I was still hearing those comments from behind my studio shelves, and I was still reading those hidden warnings into my ordinary studio materials. 

It's just exhausting having to repeat myself. It reminds me of trying to explain to my gallery rep why I can't just churn out three large-scale oil paintings a month. She doesn't get the process at all. She thinks you just throw paint at a canvas and call it a day, but oil paint takes forever to cure. If you varnish it too soon, it cracks, and then the whole piece is ruined. I had a piece crack on me right before a show two years ago, and I was so devastated I almost quit painting entirely. I ended up taking up pottery for a few months just to do something different. Throwing clay on a wheel is actually incredibly therapeutic, you have to be so centered and focused or the whole thing just collapses. The studio I went to had these amazing Japanese glazes that fired to this incredible metallic finish. I made this one bowl that looked like it was made of solid bronze, but my cat knocked it off the kitchen counter and shattered it. He's a menace, honestly, but I love him. He's an orange tabby, and they're known for being a little chaotic. He always tries to drink my paint water if I don't cover it up... 

Anyway, I really hope that finally answers it for you, because I don't think I can explain that month any differently.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms are better explained by a purely psychotic disorder versus a mood disorder with psychotic features, by clarifying a past major depressive episode.
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed or lost interest or pleasure in things?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of a major depressive episode (depressed mood or anhedonia), which is not present in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, not really. I mean, I don't think I've ever had a time where I just felt completely down or stopped caring about things for weeks on end. Even when things get stressful, I usually still want to paint or go to the studio. The studio is like my sanctuary, you know? It gets incredible morning light because it faces east, which is so rare to find in the city without paying a fortune. I got really lucky with the lease because the landlord didn't realize how much he could charge for those floor-to-ceiling windows. The only problem is that they're single-pane glass, so it gets freezing in the winter. I have to run this little space heater constantly, and I'm always terrified it's going to short out and start a fire. My friend Sarah had a space heater start a fire in her apartment a few years ago, and she lost almost everything. She had to move back in with her parents in Connecticut, which was a total nightmare for her because her mom is super critical about everything she does. She's always telling her she needs to get a "real job" instead of doing freelance graphic design. It's so toxic. I could never live with my parents again. 

But no, to answer your question, I haven't really had a period like that where I felt depressed or lost interest in stuff.

doctor.intent: To determine whether the illness has ever occurred without mood episodes entirely, which would distinguish schizoaffective disorder from bipolar disorder with psychotic features.
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when your hallucinations or strange beliefs continued while you had no manic or depressed symptoms at all?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: There was a quieter month when I was sleeping more normally and not feeling unstoppable, but I still kept hearing comments from behind the shelves and reading hidden warnings into ordinary studio materials for several weeks.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking again if the psychotic symptoms (hallucinations or strange beliefs) occurred for at least two weeks without manic or depressed symptoms, which maps directly to Additional Requirement 3.

patient.answer:
Are you seriously asking me this again? I feel like I'm losing my mind here, Doc, because I swear I have answered this exact same question like five times today. Yes. Like I said, there was a quieter month where my mood was totally normal. I was sleeping fine, I wasn't manic or depressed or feeling unstoppable. But for several weeks during that exact same time, I was still hearing those comments coming from behind the shelves, and I was still reading those hidden warnings into my studio materials. 

I just... I don't understand why we keep circling back to this. It's like talking to my internet provider. Every time I call them because the Wi-Fi in my studio drops out, they ask me if I've tried unplugging the router and plugging it back in. Like, obviously I've tried that. I'm not an idiot. But they have this script they have to read from, and they won't actually send a technician out until you jump through all their little hoops. It's so frustrating because I need the internet to upload photos of my work to my portfolio site. If my site isn't updated, curators think I'm not producing anything, which is completely untrue. I just finished a massive diptych last week. It's mostly cadmium red, which is such a difficult color to photograph accurately. Digital cameras always blow out the reds and make them look completely flat. You really have to shoot in RAW and color correct everything in Lightroom, which takes hours. I used to have a friend who was a professional photographer do it for me, but he moved to Berlin last year to open a gallery. I miss him, he always knew exactly how to light my textured pieces so the shadows popped just right. 

But anyway, yes, for the millionth time, I had a few weeks where I was totally stable but still hearing the voices and seeing the warnings. Please tell me we can move on now.

opening_question.intent: Open the interview and identify the patient's main concern.
opening_question.question: Hello, I'm glad you came in. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview shows a sustained psychotic syndrome with prominent hallucinations and delusional ideas occurring both during mood episodes and for at least 2 weeks in the absence of manic or depressive symptoms. Mood episodes are present for most of the illness, and the mood component is clearly manic/expansive with decreased need for sleep, pressured/overproductive behavior, and marked functional impairment. Because the mood episodes are manic rather than depressive, the best diagnosis is schizoaffective disorder, manic type (F25.0).
